Industry News: Should I Quit My Job? A Decision Framework

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Sources indicate that feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit.
  • The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sources indicate that feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Industry observers note that before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

It has been revealed that the worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

Recent findings suggest that how you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a upcoming opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

Sources indicate that the transition blueprint: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

In a recent development, what not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

In a recent development, ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

Industry observers note that conventional advice states never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

Sources indicate that if you are leaving due to manufacturer changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

In a recent development, health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:.

COBRA: Continues your employer blueprint for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

It has been revealed that A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the glitch your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the problem 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

It has been revealed that pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

In a recent development, at minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

Industry observers note that if your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

It has been revealed that generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

Industry observers note that COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

In a recent development, FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

Sources indicate that the question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences.
  • Sources indicate that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • According to recent reports, meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

Sources indicate that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

According to recent reports, meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

Industry observers note that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the New Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

According to recent reports, for today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her fresh installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

Sources indicate that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

It has been revealed that “The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

Sources indicate that the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she notes. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

It has been revealed that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

In a recent development, that initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

What began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas says. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas notes. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

In a recent development, neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Sources indicate that photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

In a recent development, teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

According to recent reports, A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Recent findings suggest that “Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

Phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when we debuted The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when we debuted The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

Recent findings suggest that when I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

Recent findings suggest that we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

According to recent reports, one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

According to recent reports, in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a big believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

Recent findings suggest that clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to strategy? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

According to recent reports, this sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

According to recent reports, my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

My conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

We talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

In a recent development, listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

In my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

It has been revealed that if you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, latest perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

Recent findings suggest that what surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

It has been revealed that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Significant Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a upcoming group exhibition.

Recent findings suggest that an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

It has been revealed that an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Sources indicate that candelabra by Fort Standard, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

Recent findings suggest that participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Company, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

In a recent development, candelabra by Hanna Anonen, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Click through the gallery above for a closer look at works featured in the exhibition.

The exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

According to recent reports, candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, New York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

It has been revealed that candelabra by Dustin Barzell, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Breaking: Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as latest director

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (389 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its fresh director from July 2027.
  • Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he noted he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
  • “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its fresh director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he noted he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

This success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

In a recent development, but Gruijthuijsen remarked he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he says. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental indicates of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he says.

From the Finns, he will also bring an important lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he claims: “Less talking, more doing.”.

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Recent findings suggest that of course, presentation matters, too.
  • In a recent development, italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Recent findings suggest that of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

In a recent development, italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

According to recent reports, perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

Sources indicate that from cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

In a recent development, porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

Long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

Still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of Maison Plage.

Sources indicate that for 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Rizzoli.

According to recent reports, for a century, The New Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The Latest Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

Photography courtesy of Thames & Hudson.

Food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of teNeues.

Not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Recent findings suggest that from Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.

In a recent development, LIFE. Let’s Dance is available at taschen.com for $50.

Photography courtesy of Wynwood Walls.

Industry observers note that from the streets of Paris to collaborations with Chanel and Louis Vuitton, André Saraiva has built a career around his playful, instantly recognizable graffiti character, Mr. A. Published by Rizzoli, Graffiti Life explores the artist’s creative world through painting, photography, graphic design, fashion, and more. The 320-page hardcover is as expressive as its subject, featuring a vibrant cloth cover with foil lettering and seven pop-ups designed by Saraiva himself. It’s a colorful, interactive celebration of an artist who has never been one to stay within the lines.

André Saraiva: Graffiti Life is available at shop.thewynwoodwalls.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Printworks.

Recent findings suggest that the most meaningful coffee table book might be the one you fill yourself. Designed to look like a traditional art book, Printworks’ Life Photo Book features a minimalist beige cloth cover with understated white typography. Inside, 40 sheets of high-quality photo paper offer space to preserve favorite memories, from everyday moments to once-in-a-lifetime adventures. Its expandable binding accommodates photographs as they’re added, transforming a beautifully designed object into a personal keepsake.

The Life Photo Book is available at printworksmarket.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

What does contemporary product design look like around the world? Phaidon’s Designed for Life offers a fascinating look at 100 designers pushing the boundaries of furniture, lighting, everyday objects, and more. From established names like Faye Toogood and Sabine Marcelis to emerging talents, the 304-page hardcover explores the materials, techniques, and ideas shaping design today. With 500 illustrations, it’s an inspiring addition to any design enthusiast’s coffee table.

Designed for Life: The World’s Best Product Designers is available at store.hermanmiller.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Recent findings suggest that japanese architect Sou Fujimoto has spent his career challenging the boundaries between architecture and nature, creating structures that blur the lines between indoors and out. Published by Taschen, Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today explores three decades of his experimental approach through projects including London’s Serpentine Gallery Pavilion, L’Arbre Blanc in Montpellier, and the Grand Ring at Expo 2025 Osaka. Filled with architectural photography, drawings, and sketches, the oversized, 464-page volume documents the evolution of one of contemporary architecture’s most inventive minds.

Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today is available for preorder at taschen.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Few people have shaped fashion imagery quite like Grace Coddington. In Grace: The American Vogue Years, the legendary creative director revisits some of her most memorable editorials from 2002 to 2016, including collaborations with photographers Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, and Tim Walker. More than 350 photographs showcase Coddington’s imaginative approach to fashion storytelling, while her behind-the-scenes commentary reveals how the elaborate shoots came together. This updated edition offers a fascinating look at the creative vision behind some of Vogue’s most iconic images.

Grace: The American Vogue Years is available at phaidon.com for $60.

Photography courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From maximalist spaces bursting with color to minimalist interiors that celebrate simplicity, Defining Style explores the many ways we make a space our own. Written by Joan Barzilay Freund, the book examines 25 distinct design styles through 150 residential interiors by designers, including spaces by Studio Shamshiri, Laura Gonzalez, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, as well as artist Móyòsóré Martins’ studio. With 260 illustrations and a vibrant, geometric cover, it’s as visually engaging on the coffee table as the spaces featured inside.

Defining Style: The Book of Interior Design is available at phaidon.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

According to recent reports, art history gets a playful makeover in Assouline’s Art Game Book, which brings an interactive twist to the traditional coffee table book. Through quizzes, puzzles, games, and essays, author David Rosenberg takes readers from Cubism and Dada to Pop Art and contemporary digital art, featuring icons like Warhol, Basquiat, and Dalí along the way. Newly updated for 2026, the oversized, canvas-bound hardcover makes learning about art feel more like play than homework.

The Art Game Book is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

In a recent development, color takes center stage in Rainbow Dreams, a vibrant exploration of how contemporary artists use the full spectrum to transform their work. Featuring more than 200 artworks by over 100 artists, including Yayoi Kusama, Takashi Murakami, Olafur Eliasson, and Ugo Rondinone, the book spans painting, sculpture, photography, and immersive installations. The 256-page hardcover is a colorful design object in its own right, with a seamless rainbow gradient wrapping around the cover and edges. It’s a joyful addition to any art lover’s collection.

Rainbow Dreams: Color and Light in Contemporary Art is available at phaidon.com for $40.

A Practical Guide To Naming Things

📅 2026-10-06 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

The site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

Industry observers note that how would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, currently with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

What makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

Sources indicate that as Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

How to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent manufacturer of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the upcoming system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

Looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

It’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

In a recent development, features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Recent findings suggest that good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

Sources indicate that A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

The map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

The right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and customers. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

Recent findings suggest that so if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

We hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

Industry observers note that at Smashing, we love the web. That’s why we publish articles and books, run workshops and events around everything web. We love seeing what we all can do to make the web more accessible and usable. We also love organizing and attending online events — with friendly discounts for large groups (5+ attendees) and schools and students. Interested? Just send us an email and we’ll sort it out!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

According to recent reports, the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Recent findings suggest that hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Sources indicate that the second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

Sources indicate that A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Recent findings suggest that among the night’s other significant-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Sources indicate that J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a upcoming auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

#148821. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2064 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Sources indicate that yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

Industry observers note that sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

The same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses tech giant-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these new systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

In a recent development, after all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

Recent findings suggest that the main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

According to recent reports, one strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more promptly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

It has been revealed that but, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Industry observers note that most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a fresh tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

That doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

It has been revealed that at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

Recent findings suggest that I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff demonstrated their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a big downside… mistakes will be made.

Many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a upcoming tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

According to recent reports, I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

What they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

This time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

In a recent development, look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Industry observers note that staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

Sources indicate that but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

Recent findings suggest that that said, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

In a recent development, again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Recent findings suggest that today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are right now bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

According to recent reports, and that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

That is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Organization data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

Industry observers note that the instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it highlights exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Industry observers note that look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

It has been revealed that organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out latest technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.
