💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.
  • The church will occupy a right now underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.
  • The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a right now underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” remarked Ban.

Sources indicate that “The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a upcoming sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”.

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four fresh churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

Sources indicate that its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped strategy, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios remarked will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

According to recent reports, the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in Fresh Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

📅 03 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry.
  • The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience.
  • For many, tattoos are much more than art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

It has been revealed that anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

Industry observers note that but here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Industry observers note that getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

In a recent development, psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

According to recent reports, there’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

Industry observers note that one 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos revealed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Sources indicate that tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings indicated that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every open-world game has a crowd problem. Pack the streets with people and, sooner or later, you clock the same jogger for the fifth time, and the illusion falls apart. GTA 6 breaks that wall and delivers a world filled with unique little virtual actors.

Having spent time in Leonida myself for my GTA 6 review, often just people-watching, eavesdropping on conversations, and spying on the game's background actors as they play out their lives, I can say this is the most alive game I've played. A regular couple rant about gentrification and other conspiracies on their apartment steps; two others argue about that latest Manatees result; two women sip coffee, gossiping about their friend's love life; one's eyes widen, brows lift, just a fraction too slowly to feel like shock.

With all I've seen, I can see why Rockstar's art team is so keen to talk about its pedestrians and background characters.

Valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, indicates Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

In a recent development, garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also claims it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

Garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also notes it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

Sources indicate that mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, conveys the scale. “There are close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities,” he claims, “then we layer in hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences to punctuate the world and reward exploration.”.

According to recent reports, those everyday sets, with people hanging out and doing day-to-day jobs, “form the foundation of this living world”, according to Tennant. The variety extends to bodies, too. The team decided early to “really push the variation in character sizes and body types”, which meant building “a very robust way to share animations between characters”.

Garcia says the team built upcoming technology and tools “from the ground up” for the engine. The all-new in-house tech covers hair, cloth simulation and head-and-body customisation, and it’s applied across the world “to benefit all characters equally”. So the people on the street get the same tech as the leads.

It’s the little things that sell it. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, indicates that “everywhere you look, little stories constantly unfold”. That might be as simple as what someone’s wearing, how they walk and talk, or what they’re blasting from a passing car.

Industry observers note that I see this in how characters dress and behave differently across the map. Some things are just obvious, such as characters wearing swimsuits on the beach, but Rockstar takes it further, as Leonida's beachgoers lie and chat on towels, play frisbee, and make mistakes – I snuck onto a boat party and watched as characters danced and reacted to Lucia and Jason's moves.

Most of the people you pass in Leonida will only be on screen for a moment, but Rockstar has built them as if you might stop and look; in fact, the developer wants you to stop, look and listen, and simply love being in the world. Sam Fender's People Watching is on the soundtrack for a reason.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian rolled out Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.
  • Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal.
  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins notes about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of significant butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal problems and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins indicates about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

Industry observers note that “She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins indicates you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in latest people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

In a recent development, coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins claims change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins claims, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

Breaking: ‘I want the experiences I had to be available forever’: arts figures and scientists hit out at proposed job cuts at Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution.
  • Recent findings suggest that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium.
  • Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

Recent findings suggest that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

Staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”.

“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and Newly introduced Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

The proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a plan to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

Industry observers note that although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a newly introduced organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry says. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

It has been revealed that asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he says.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

In a recent development, according to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a newly introduced government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, states Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

Recent findings suggest that A state government spokesperson states there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a fresh A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”.

In a recent development, the proposed cuts to staff numbers are currently under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both problems are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have said they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

This beautiful logo design was created to grow like nature

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that how do you rebrand a 200-year-old institution that wants its new logo to "feel like plants"?
  • And yet the upcoming identity for the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society achieves it.
  • Turning 200 years old in 2027, the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society is only 50 years younger than the US as an independent country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that how do you rebrand a 200-year-old institution that wants its new logo to "feel like plants"? Plants are constantly changing; they grow, wilt, bloom, move in the wind, shed their leaves and sprout new ones. Captivating that in a permanent identity built to last years might seem like an impossible task.

And yet the upcoming identity for the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society achieves it. The logo is a clear candidate as one of the best animated logos, and the blooming rebrand also includes one of the most beautiful brand manuals I've seen. There's even a flipbook, further demonstrating the dynamism of the mark.

Turning 200 years old in 2027, the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society is only 50 years younger than the US as an independent country. To mark its upcoming anniversary, it brought in local design agency Smith & Diction to create an identity that better represents the breadth of what it does, from urban greening to landscaping parks and the City Harvest initiative.

It has been revealed that the existing logo design was fairly generic. It could have been the identity for a financial institution – or even a retirement home, as Smith & Diction point out. Depicting a single tree, it hardly represented the rich diversity of the plant kingdom. What kind of tree was it supposed to be anyway?

The agency's solution was a three-letter logo in which the letters become roots, with a different species of native plant growing from each. Smith & Diction states the process began with the illustrations. Summer McClure drew the plants and flowers within rectangles, chosen to represent Philadelphia's grid layout of city blocks.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Industry observers note that the logo was then animated. Henrique Barone drew the plants growing from the letterforms, frame by frame. This allowed the creation of the flipbook (see the Instagram post below) as well as the final animation, which feels like a timelapse video from a nature documentary. A second animation was made by Justin Lawes to show the plants moving as if swaying in the breeze.

The result is a strong, versatile and dynamic logo that represents nature, the city grid, and the PHS's work to unite them.

A post shared by Smith & Diction — Design & Copywriting (@smith_diction).

According to recent reports, the logo's backed up by further custom brand illustrations based on native flora for social posts and things like menus and signs. There are also floral illustrations for sub brands, including a peony for the PHS's annual flower show.

Industry observers note that the beauty of this system is that it introduces another way in which the branding can grow like a garden. The idea is that the PHS can host workshops where people will be able to draw their own florals to fit the same dimensions, or make their own linocut prints.

According to recent reports, the colour palette is also unconventional, again reflecting the diversity of plant life. While there's a core set of greens and blues, the palette expands to contemplate dozens of colours. As for type, Caslon Doric is the lead, backed up by the elegance of ES Park, a choice inspired by the practical simplicity of old PHS exhibition posters.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

It's one of those projects that's blurs the line between brand design and art. That's apparent in the decision to produce a physical brand book, which was "designed as a reminder to touch grass and hold books".

"Making a shiny digital case study to talk about our partnership just felt inauthentic," Smith & Diction explains. "This isn’t a shiny digital brand, it’s rooted in the tangible: grass below your feet, warm sun on your face, the sound of birds chirping to one another from neighboring trees.".

You can purchase a copy of the book for $60 for which you also get the flip book, a lapel pin and a poster.

According to recent reports, joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

Art Basel Hong Kong has confirmed the 232 exhibitors that will participate in its upcoming 2027 edition, scheduled to run March 25–27, with VIP preview days on March 23–24, at the.

Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre.

The upcoming fair has contracted slightly, with 2027 having eight fewer exhibitors than the 240 the fair had in 2026. (Both figures do not include the Zero 10 participants.) Similarly, the main Galleries section will have 171 participants, down from 182 in 2027, while Discoveries (for emerging artists and galleries) has stayed constant at 25. Insights (curated presentations for Asia-Pacific artists) and Echoes (for work made in the past five years) will both have 18 exhibitors; in 2026, Insights had 20 and Echoes 13. Related Articles Art Basel Miami Beach Names 272 Exhibitors, With a Major Overhaul to the Fair's Floor Plan NADA Miami Names 135 Exhibitors for Upcoming Edition in December.

Like the Miami Beach fair next week, the 2027 Hong Kong iteration will also feature a latest floor proposal. The four special sections—Discoveries, Insights, Echoes, and Zero 10—will move to a different floor from the Galleries section, giving the smaller sections “greater space and visibility, while enhancing opportunities for discovery through a thoughtfully curated visitor journey,” per a release.

Industry observers note that the fair will also have 31 first-time exhibitors, with 14 of them making their debuts in the Discoveries section. Newcomers to the Galleries section include Galerie Nordenhake, Yares Art, Richard Saltoun Gallery, Matthew Brown, and VeneKlasen, while Kayokoyuki, Good Weather, Make Room, and Temnikova & Kasela will be first timers in Discoveries. Five galleries will return after a hiatus, including Marian Goodman Gallery, Goodman Gallery, and Vadehra Art Gallery.

Industry observers note that more than half of the exhibitors have spaces in the Asia-Pacific region, with 27 having locations in Hong Kong, like 10 Chancery Lane Gallery, Blindspot Gallery, Empty Gallery, Kiang Malingue, Ora-Ora, and Rossi & Rossi. Other geographical areas with strong showing are Mainland China (32 exhibitors), Japan (20), South Korea (16), and Taiwan (8). International blue-chip galleries include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Pace Gallery, White Cube, Gladstone, Lisson, Thaddaeus Ropac, Esther Schipper, and Sprüth Magers.

The Encounters section for large-scale works will be organized by Mami Kataoka, with Isabella Tam, Alia Swastika, and Hirokazu Tokuyama, while Zero 10 will be done for the first time by Sunny Cheung, an independent curator and former curator of design and architecture at M+. Artist Ellen Pau will once again organize the Film section. Details for these sections will be revealed at a later date.

“The most important and innovative dialogues emerge at the intersection of different worlds, where artistic, cultural, and business communities come together to generate new ideas, perspectives, and opportunities for exchange. As Asia continues to shape the global cultural landscape, Art Basel Hong Kong provides a platform for these connections to flourish,” ABHK director Angelle Siyang-Le said in a statement.

Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for Dezeen's 20x20 project

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler.
  • The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.
  • “I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

The duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Significant Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

According to recent reports, “We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

According to recent reports, “The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

It has been revealed that humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and stated that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” noted Bergh.

Industry observers note that our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

“But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

“Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” stated Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most key thing,” she continued.

Sources indicate that “Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

Recent findings suggest that the hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

It has been revealed that “The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

“You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo remarked funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

“All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

Industry observers note that “It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have prepares for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

In a recent development, “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the story is a dystopia with a twist, set around the idea that resources have run out, humans have retreated into a simulation, and the robots left behind to look after the physical world have started to find beauty in it.
  • Recent findings suggest that the big draw of Unreal Engine 5 was speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when your physical set is three walls and a ceiling, whatever’s outside the window has to carry a lot of the film. For SNTIENT 2.0, the Fashion Innovation Agency’s film for London College of Fashion, that view was a bleak, abandoned city, and it lived entirely in Unreal Engine.

In a recent development, the story is a dystopia with a twist, set around the idea that resources have run out, humans have retreated into a simulation, and the robots left behind to look after the physical world have started to find beauty in it. “That gave us our visual starting point. A bleak, oppressive sci-fi environment with the potential for transformation,” states Dickon Knowles, director of content at Dandelion + Burdock. The finished film doesn't explore that transformation as far as originally planned, but the city still set the tone for everything else.

Recent findings suggest that the big draw of Unreal Engine 5 was speed. Working in a real-time engine meant the team could play with spaces, lighting, and textures, see the result straight away, and change it on the spot, instead of waiting for a render only to find it was wrong. “It made the whole process much more fluid,” Knowles says.

According to recent reports, other routes were tried first. “We tried a couple of generative approaches to creating the city plate for the wall, but resolutions were an issue and the visual fidelity wasn’t there,” Knowles explains. “Which is why we reverted back to our existing Unreal Engine version.”.

In a recent development, even then, the city needed work. The original environment was foggy and slightly desaturated, and wasn't reading through the camera as intended. Knowles reworked the fog, replacing the general wash through the scene with more detailed VDB fog, while reducing its overall presence and boosting the saturation, particularly in the city windows. The LED wall looked better with richer blacks and more contrast, which the fog had been fighting against. It needed a more vivid backdrop to work on camera.

Recent findings suggest that most of the city was already built before the shoot, with the team making visual refinements, grading and subtle tweaks on set. It wasn't building a digital world from scratch while the cameras were rolling. The advantage was seeing how those changes looked on the wall and through the camera, and making adjustments without waiting for a fresh render.

The city also ran on an LED wall as the view from the character’s window, which gave the performer something real to react to rather than a green screen to imagine over.

Cinematographer Ben Saffer, whose firm, Supervision VP, handled the virtual production, states the appeal was being able to capture everything together. The virtual and physical lighting could be controlled as one, so the glow on screen matched the light on set. “You’re doing it all in camera and capturing everything together at once, and you’re not having to guess at anything,” he says.

According to recent reports, the alternatives were a green screen or a pre-rendered backdrop. Knowles says cost was less of a concern than visual quality, because the city content had already been created for a previous project. “The city lights reflect on the performer’s face and on the surfaces of the props and set,” he says. “There is a level of visual immersion that is hard to capture in a studio without the LED wall to illuminate the space.”.

It has been revealed that the LED wall wasn't simply providing something pretty to look at outside the window; it was lighting the performer and the physical set at the same time, similar to how Magnopus used Unreal Engine for Fallout. The intention was to keep post-production to a minimum, getting the footage as close to the finished shot as possible during filming.

Unreal also solved a budget problem because the film needed a shutter that rises to reveal the city, but a moving shutter built into the set wasn't realistic on the budget, and adding one in VFX would have meant losing that in-camera moment.

According to recent reports, so the LED wall became the shutter, rising to reveal the digital city behind it. For reverse shots, a second wall on wheels could be brought in to act as a fourth wall. Because the content ran in real time, the team could swiftly render new assets for those angles, animate them, and get them moving. “It was nice to get that in camera,” Saffer says.

In a recent development, not everything went virtual, though, as the pod itself was a physical build, because the team wanted it to feel gritty and lived-in, with the LED wall and Unreal handling the distant environment. The AI-generated dream sequence at the start was a separate part of the production, created using generative tools to show the character floating in water before she wakes up.

According to recent reports, the film has very few beats: the character wakes, the window opens, she looks out. Saffer says the real challenge was getting a sense of the world and her place in it within two minutes. The team also had to make the most of the tiny space, shooting on an URSA Cine 17K 65 with prototype Atlas Lens Co. anamorphic lenses. The larger sensor meant Saffer could capture more of the set without resorting to an extreme wide-angle lens, which would have distorted the perspective.

There was still room for a bit of old-fashioned experimentation. Towards the end of the film, as the character looks towards the window, Saffer held a plastic Polly Pocket toy in front of the lens and shone his phone torch through it from the side to create an optical effect. He also played around with cling film and other materials in front of the lens.

Lucy Sante Talks About What Collage Enables That Writing Can’t

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lucy Sante started making collages long before she established herself as a writer of incisive theories of photography (see Walker Evans, from 1999, Evidence, from 1992, and 2009’s Folk Photography: The American Real-Photo Postcard 1905–1930); of urban studies (see Low Life: Lures and Snares of Old New York, her 1991 chronicle of the city’s underworlds); and of personal history (2024’s I Heard Her Call My Name: A Memoir of Transition).
  • Sources indicate that over the decades, Sante devoted herself most fervently to writing, with a focus on photography: In 2023, she retired as a professor of writing and the history of photography at Bard College.
  • What do you remember about your early collages that made you want to keep making them?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lucy Sante started making collages long before she established herself as a writer of incisive theories of photography (see Walker Evans, from 1999, Evidence, from 1992, and 2009’s Folk Photography: The American Real-Photo Postcard 1905–1930); of urban studies (see Low Life: Lures and Snares of Old New York, her 1991 chronicle of the city’s underworlds); and of personal history (2024’s I Heard Her Call My Name: A Memoir of Transition). As a teenage émigré in the 1960s, she would clip and assemble images from magazines, a practice she has continued on and off ever since—drawing lasting inspiration from the metaphysical juxtapositions of René Magritte, a fellow Belgian. As a clerk at the Strand, a storied used bookshop in New York, she began working with a wider range of materials, from cast-off paperbacks and technical manuals to medical textbooks and other arcane publications. All the while, she developed a mysterious and poetic style of collage that mixed imagery from different eras and suggested the outlines of stories, however elusive those might be. Related Articles Ralph Lemon Talks about Dance, Drawing, and Maintaining a Decades-Long Generative Practice Steve Locke Talks About His Painterly and Polemical Provocations.

Sources indicate that over the decades, Sante devoted herself most fervently to writing, with a focus on photography: In 2023, she retired as a professor of writing and the history of photography at Bard College. Her newest book, My Heart & I Agree (2026), is an essay collection that covers subjects including Surrealist photography, cowboy iconography, and Soul Train. There, her keen eye toward camera culture remains evident. She refocused some of her energies on collage in recent years, and her visual work featured this past spring in solo exhibitions at Picture Theory in Chelsea and at the American Academy of Arts and Letters in upper Manhattan, where an early collage from the ’70s joined works made since 2020. From her home in upstate Fresh York, Sante spoke with A.i.A. about learning to look through magazines, moving her way into fine-art collage, and finding poetry in images she gives new life.

What do you remember about your early collages that made you want to keep making them?

I had two sources of materials for my earliest collages: a stack of Arizona Highways magazines from the 1950s and early ’60s, and my parents’ subscription to Life. I remember a collage that I made featuring Jimi Hendrix and a mushroom cloud: That was hip. I was imitating collages I saw—not artistic collages, but collages in popular media. In the early Rolling Stone, on the letters page, almost every week they’d have a collage by this graphic designer named Wilfried Sätty, whose house I stayed in years later, after his death in 1982. He had a particular style: outer space plus old engravings.

Had you made other kinds of visual art?

Industry observers note that I’m colorblind, and that was a big problem for me. I drew, but had to work in black and white. I wasn’t that bad—just not as good as I wanted to be. In high school, I started making band flyers, which I continued when I was living on the Lower East Side in the 1970s and ’80s. I made several for the Del-Byzanteens, a band I also wrote lyrics for. Many people in the band became celebrated in one way or another: Jim Jarmusch as a filmmaker, Jamie Nares as a painter, and Phil Kline as a composer.

How did your work at the Strand Bookstore find its way into your collages?

We started a collective publication called Stranded that was originally going to be like a workers’ gripe sheet. But instead, we published art and poetry and stuff like that. I had collage-like things in all four issues. Within a week of my starting, Fred Bass [fabled owner of the Strand] named me the paperback department—I was the entire department all by myself. Bookmen in that period did not take paperbacks seriously and just put them out in the 25-cent carts. That meant I had to deal with romance books, and when I put those out on Thursdays, they were mobbed by old ladies, and it was a nightmare. But it also meant that whenever they bought a library, they would throw me everything that wasn’t a hardcover book, including magazines, maps, postcards, and all kinds of stuff that I took home and still have. I made collages recently with material I acquired back then at the Strand.

What was the Strand like as a downtown institution then compared to now?

In a recent development, nobody was very literary on the Lower East Side in the ’70s. People were starting bands and making movies. There wasn’t even painting at the time. We had to wait for Basquiat. In the ’70s, we had some bad poets, a few bad essayists. Nobody [in the neighborhood] wrote fiction. But at that point, the sociology was nothing to compare to now, because you could waltz into Newly introduced York City hitchhiking from Denver or somewhere and find yourself a cheap apartment and get a job at the Strand. Your salary would pay your rent, and you had money left over to go clubbing. That’s long gone now.

What were you looking for? What made something conducive to collage?

I liked texture and was really interested in contrasting eras. I liked faded color. I was taking inspiration from a lot of different sources. Of the flyers I made for the Del-Byzanteens, one of them [drew from] massive posters that a syndicate put out to try to promote a science-fiction comic strip. I X-Acto–knifed out the thought balloons and filled them in with other material. That was because I had a friend who’d just come over from Paris with a Situationist International book, and I got inspired by that.

In a recent development, you mentioned beginning with an interest in popular-media collage. What art world collagists interested you later on?

Recent findings suggest that I was inspired by Max Ernst and Robert Rauschenberg. I found a book by Jess, Robert Duncan’s partner and a great collage artist. I discovered Bruce Conner and, of course, the Surrealists and Dadaists—Berlin Dada, especially, with John Heartfield and Hannah Höch. And the Russians, like El Lissitzky and Alexander Rodchenko. There’s a whole world of collage out there.

How would you describe your decision-making process?

There are collages that I don’t quite know how to resolve. They might need something else, but I don’t know what. Often they’re just made on the spot.

One work that especially caught my eye in your Arts and Letters show was De La (2023). How did you arrive upon the composition for that?

It has been revealed that that’s my favorite work of mine. That’s one I’m keeping. It just came together in a particular way, and it zinged. And I can take you through exactly how I made it, because I do remember. The materials go back to 1981, which was the tail end of people selling shit on the street on the Lower East Side. There had been this kind of ad hoc 24/7 flea market around Astor Place. One night, I was walking down St. Marks Place, and there was a guy selling damaged posters. I bought a shopping bag’s worth for 10 bucks; they were all falling to pieces. The yellow and white in De La is from a poster for an early movie by the Italian director Elio Petri, and the lettering comes from miscellaneous papers from a local auction up here [in upstate Upcoming York]. It had all kinds of crap, including a poster for a touring Laurel and Hardy anthology film in Spanish. The tire at the top comes from a French car magazine from the ’30s, and the chrysanthemum comes from a seed-company ad in Life. The glove is from a 1950s Punch, a humor magazine that had wonderful advertising. And then the star of the show is the woman with the fingerprints on her back, which I’d been saving up for the longest time. It comes from a French soft-porn magazine from the ’30s. It was magic how they all came together.

What do letters and different bits of text do for you in collage work?

There’s lettering in, I’d say, 95 percent of my collages, and that’s partly because I kind of think of them as movie posters. One of my original inspirations was the posters I saw when I first started going to the movies as a child, for films like Ben Hur (1959) and Hawaii (1966). They had enormous, sculpted letters for the title, and then there would be little figures swirling around them illustrating the scope of the story. In a way, everything I do refers back to those.

In a recent development, are there writerly aspects to the collage-making process for you? They can’t help but suggest some sort of narrative for the viewer, but I don’t know about the maker, necessarily….

It’s ambiguity central. I started life, so to speak, as a poet. I later realized I was a prose writer, but poetry is at the heart of everything for me. Among other things, that means making a structure from a sort of lean-to of ambiguities—one ambiguity resting on another, all suggesting a story and all suggesting a meaning but never actually giving it to you. If I make a collage and it seems to have a legible message, I have failed.

What makes you turn to collage instead of writing when a creative impulse strikes?

It’s something I feel in my hands—like, “By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked this way comes.” It’s the feeling that I need to make something. Being a writer does not involve the body the way that making visual art does, and I have that craving. I wanted to be an artist before I ever thought of being a writer.

Because I have so much to do right now, I’m not running down to the basement to make more collages. But in the meantime, I’ve bought things on eBay. I bought a bunch of 19th-century chromolithographs I’m eager to use, and somebody sold me these incredibly dirty comics—I don’t mean dirty like sexy, but dirty like they were lying in a crawl space for 75 years. I like dirt. I like fading. I like things that are crinkled, things that are ripped. I prefer things that are damaged, because they carry their histories. They establish a custodial chain and have a lot of dead people’s fingerprints on them. If something looks like it comes out of the box, even if it was published in 1922, I’m far less interested than if it’s fucked up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sources indicate that sleep is the best way to help your body recover swiftly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Significant disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

It has been revealed that stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing challenges. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

According to recent reports, light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

It has been revealed that working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

Recent findings suggest that an occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

In a recent development, diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

According to recent reports, once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Industry observers note that regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that formnext is the world’s biggest additive manufacturing trade show, gathering the best 3D printer manufacturers, large and small, to show off their latest goods in Germany each year. And this year was a blast.

Recent findings suggest that the event is open to the public, but the true purpose of the show is for businesses, factories and retailers to come and do some shopping. This year the show shrank to three halls from the usual four, with consumer grade 3D printing having a larger presence than ever before.

My maker’s heart sang at all the new desktop 3D printers now available, from some of the best CNC machines to the cutting edge in UV machines, to trusty glitter coated plastic!

But AI had to go and make its presence known! It stamped a huge footprint at the show, and response was predictably mixed.

The shocker this year is the SnowPod, a prosumer desktop metal printer that uses a laser to melt thin layers of steel powder within a chamber of nitrogen. It’s launching soon on Kickstarter with a VIP price starting at $4999. Printing in metal is tricky stuff, with more safety hazards to overcome than FDM or resin. The metal dust is not only flammable, but hazardous to breathe, but SnowX seems to have a handle on safety protocols.

I counted eight completely new tool changers, plus two more that debuted last year at Formnext. Prusa, Bambu, Snapmaker, Elegoo, Creality, and Flashforge now have tool changers from four to nine tools, with Anycubic being the lone single nozzle holdout. Crowdfunding hopefuls Axiloop, Co Print and WonderMaker have entered the chat, with nozzle maker Phaetus tagging along with the new Hydra system. Bambu’s H3C is currently the machine to beat, shipping with 8 normal tools and one bonus 2.85mm tool for printing super soft 75A TPU.

UV printing is gaining momentum as manufacturers figure out how to shrink massive industrial machines into desktop printers that are more affordable for entrepreneurial makers. Being able to 3D print full color resin miniatures is enticing, but I’m worried that newbies will be blindsided by the hidden cost of printhead replacement. These easily cloggable printheads are similar to what you see in a paper ink jet printer, but easily cost $900 to replace. And it’s not a question of if you’ll need to replace it, but when.

It has been revealed that prusa Research's newest innovation wasn’t a 3D printer, but a new way to run one. Prusa Connect Local keeps your printers off the internet without resorting to sneaker net and a USB stick. It’s similar to LAN mode, but runs off a local server so you can coordinate jobs for a whole print farm. The server can be as simple as a Raspberry Pi and your “farm” could be a fleet CORE One or a pair of MK4S. The software is free to download, open source and currently just for Prusa machines. I’m guessing that will change as the tech nerds start tinkering.

AI integration in 3D printing is inevitable, and quite useful in some cases. I don’t mind if my printer is monitoring print fails with a smart camera, or if my 3D scanner uses AI to clean up a model. But things get complicated when AI takes over the creative process of model design. Some say AI modeling is no different than cameras taking the job of painters…but is it? Hi3D and Tripo both had impressive booths to sway consumers to their side.

Recent findings suggest that denise is a tech reviewer, content creator, and former newspaper reporter with over 20 years of journalism experience. She's tested well over one hundred 3D printers and lasers for Tom's Hardware, and has traveled the world looking for the best tech to share with her readers. You're most likely to find her at a maker festival with her 3D printed RC Death Racer, The Harley Quinn.

Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance.
  • In a recent development, creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

In a recent development, creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

It has been revealed that because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s crucial to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

Industry observers note that the same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Recent findings suggest that thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

According to recent reports, furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

According to recent reports, creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

Industry News: Hauser & Wirth Now Represents Ser Serpas, Fast-Rising Artist Who Combs the Detritus of Everyday Life

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hauser & Wirth now represents Ser Serpas, a fast-rising artist known for her poetically minded installations and haunting paintings.
  • Industry observers note that she will have her first solo show with Hauser & Wirth at its Paris space in January.
  • Born and raised in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood, Serpas is an itinerant artist who is primarily based in Paris but also “regularly moves between such cities as Latest York, Los Angeles, Geneva, and Tbilisi,” according to a release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hauser & Wirth now represents Ser Serpas, a fast-rising artist known for her poetically minded installations and haunting paintings. Hauser & Wirth will represent the artist in collaboration with her longtime gallery LC Queisser, which has spaces in Tbilisi, Georgia, and Cologne, Germany.

Industry observers note that she will have her first solo show with Hauser & Wirth at its Paris space in January. For that exhibition, Serpas will show a latest series of paintings, as well as debut a multimedia installation. Born in 1995, she is one of the youngest artists to be represented by Hauser & Wirth, and one of a handful Latinx artists to show with the gallery, which added to its roster rafa esparza earlier this month. Related Articles Hauser & Wirth Now Represents rafa esparza, Maker of Adobe Sculptures and Paintings That Center Community Frieze London Brings 400-Year-Old Paintings and Collectors in Their 20s.

Born and raised in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood, Serpas is an itinerant artist who is primarily based in Paris but also “regularly moves between such cities as Latest York, Los Angeles, Geneva, and Tbilisi,” according to a release. Her practice is equally disparate, spanning various mediums from sculpture and painting to video and photography to poetry and performance.

According to recent reports, serpas is best known for her sculptures and installations in which she brings together the detritus of everyday life, giving the found objects that comprise them new life and meaning. She gathers the items from the streets where she is living or in residency. “I’m building a palette every time I go into a new city,” she has said of her process. In a 2023 New York Times profile, she described “Parisian trash [as] sturdy.”.

To make her works, Serpas usually works alone, constructing the pieces in situ. She often tells the venues she will show at, “OK, you have to give me the key and there’s going to be a lot of things in the recycling and I might have some friends over, but you just have to trust me and you’ll get a show. But on my terms.”.

Sources indicate that often, these installations make poignant, if oblique, references to today’s most pressing issues. An installation for the 2024 Whitney Biennial, for example, featured a tattered US flag laying on “a disused piece of a sectional relegated to the corner—which is perhaps where the Stars and Stripes belongs during these depressing times,” as ARTnews’s Alex Greenberger wrote in his review. The 2025 work tube of brief cadavers made sadder still, which featured on ARTnews’s list of “The Defining Artworks of 2025,” combined elements that recalled the ongoing migrant crisis.

In a recent development, serpas also has an active painting practice, which often features ambiguous figures, initially depicting those of her lovers and people before and after surgery. Perhaps in a nod to her interest in horror and the uncanny, she presses two wet canvases together to create a ghost image. Since 2023, Serpas has used AI to generate the bodies that animate and distort her paintings.

It has been revealed that “For the first time, I’m showing paintings in a pretty traditional way, and I know that’s going to ask a lot from people who are familiar with my sculptural practice,” Serpas told the Art Newspaper in 2025, of her show at Kunsthalle Basel that summer. “The sculptures are difficult to contend with for many collectors and institutions, and I do wish more people had them in their homes. Some people do, but not as many as the paintings, drawings or even some of the sound-based multimedia pieces I’ve made.”.

Over the past decade, Serpas has become one of her generation’s most closely watched and in-demand artists. She has had institutional solo exhibitions at Kölnischer Kunstverein in Cologne (through December 13), Contemporary Art Gallery in Vancouver (2026), Kunsthalle Basel (2025), the Swiss Institute in Latest York (2023), and the Museum Ludwig in Cologne (2023). In addition to the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Serpas has also been included in “Flow States: La Trienal 2024” at El Museo del Barrio, “The Gatherers” (2025) at MoMA PS1, and the 2020 Made in L.A. biennial at the Hammer Museum.

According to recent reports, her work is also collected by some of the world’s top collectors, who show her pieces in their private museums. They include Maja Hoffmann’s LUMA Westbau, where she had a show in 2018; François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, where she featured in the 2021 inaugural exhibition and had a solo in 2023; Tony Salamé’s Aishti Foundation in Beirut, which included her in a group show titled “Fresh Flowers”; and a room of work at the Rubell Museum in Miami in 2025.

In a recent development, “We are delighted to begin working with Ser Serpas at this exciting juncture in her growing career,” Hauser & Wirth president Marc Payot said in a statement. “Like a number of our gallery’s foundational artists—Mike Kelley and Jason Rhoades come to mind—she is fearless in her commitment to a process-based, intermedia practice that mingles the deceptively mundane with something powerfully existential. We are excited to embrace her vision and look forward to sharing it with wider audiences.”.

#148667. How to paint anything more easily by splitting up shapes

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2120 w)
